limitations: pysystemtrade's published prices end in March 2024 and follow its own roll calendar (for crude oil and the grains it holds one contract a year); Databento's begin in 2010 and follow the most traded contract. The two are run separately, not spliced, and hold different contracts, so they are two records of the same markets, not one.
Futures returns here are excess returns: they leave out the interest earned on the cash behind a futures position, which is the same for every signal and does not change the comparisons.
Costs are a fixed estimate per market in basis points of notional per round trip, charged on every change in weight and on every roll; real costs vary with size, time and liquidity.

Carry uses the held and the next quoted contract. A deferred price unchanged for five rows in a row is treated as stale and gives no reading; when a contract's terms change (the Treasury futures' move to a 6% notional coupon in 2000) the two contracts differ in kind, and the Treasury carry readings jump for a few months then and again in late 2014 and early 2015.
A roll day on which the new contract has no previous close is left out rather than guessed; for some markets (the ultra Treasury contracts, feeder cattle, soybean meal) that is many of their rolls.

The universe is today's liquid CME markets, picked with hindsight: markets that died are not in it, which flatters any signal that is long what survived. pysystemtrade's SOFR file is back-filled with Eurodollar prices before SOFR futures existed.

Positioning needs the CFTC's site and runs only where it is reachable; positions as of Tuesday are used from the following Monday's close, and months when government shutdowns delayed the releases get no reading.

Most of these signals were published before much of the sample, so the record before publication is the one the authors saw; the record since publication is shown on its own, and it is short (four to eleven years), so a Sharpe ratio there has a standard error of 0.3 to 0.5.
findings: 38 futures markets, 2010-06 to 2026-11, 11 tests (each signal across markets and over time, net of costs), Benjamini-Hochberg at q = 0.05: 0 passed; 0 also beat a passive long portfolio of the same markets, held in both halves, within asset classes and since publication.
Of 120 runs of random persistent signals on the real returns (each market's average removed), 4% had p below 0.05 (about 5% is the honest rate).

Trend: past 12 months' return, across markets (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012): Sharpe 0.42 after costs, p 0.0670, beyond holding long 0.43; since 2013: Sharpe 0.63 over 168 months. Verdict: no better than chance.

Trend: past 1 month's return, across markets (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012): Sharpe 0.30 after costs, p 0.0895, beyond holding long 0.34; since 2013: Sharpe 0.34 over 167 months. Verdict: no better than chance.

Carry: annualized gap between the nearer and the further contract, across markets (Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen and Vrugt 2018): Sharpe 0.31 after costs, p 0.1162, beyond holding long 0.29; since 2019: Sharpe 0.26 over 96 months. Verdict: no better than chance.

Trend: past 12 months' return, over time (Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen 2012): Sharpe 0.24 after costs, p 0.1559, beyond holding long 0.25; since 2013: Sharpe 0.38 over 168 months. Verdict: no better than chance.

Hedging pressure: commercial hedgers' net short share (CFTC), over time (de Roon, Nijman and Veld 2000; Basu and Miffre 2013): Sharpe 0.20 after costs, p 0.2802, beyond holding long 0.20; since 2001: Sharpe 0.20 over 187 months. Verdict: no better than chance.
